The Drug Bizarro’s Web Page Says
"Marijuana/hashish-related emergency department episodes have increased 219%

June 30, 1998

http://www.whitehousedrugpolicy.gov/drugfact/drugtrends/emergency.html

http://www.whitehousedrugpolicy.gov/drugfact/drugtrends/emergency.html

"Emergency department data"

Since October 1, 1992, SAMHSA has sponsored the Drug Abuse Warning Network (DAWN). Earlier surveys were sponsored by the Drug Enforcement Administration, U.S. Department of Justice, and then by NIDA. Although this indicator of drug use consequences began in the early 1970s, nationally representative data are currently available only for 1978 through 1996.

The number of drug-related emergency department episodes increased from 323,100 in 1978 to an all-time high of 518,521 in 1994. Between 1994 and 1996, drug-related emergency department episodes decreased by 6% (from 518,500 to 487,600). In 1996, cocaine-related episodes comprised 30% (144,200) of all emergency department drug-related episodes. Cocaine-related episodes in 1996 were at their highest level since the DAWN survey began in 1978. Since 1990, marijuana/hashish-related episodes have increased 219% (from 15,700 to 50,000). Between 1990 and 1996, the number of heroin-related episodes has doubled (from 33,900 to 70,500).

(Ed. note: These people work so hard to avoid the truth, but this is one of those times when they have to know that they are lying. The SAMHSA emergency room numbers are not for marijuana "related" episodes, but rather for "mentions" of marijuana by people seeking treatment.

That is, when people go to the emergency room having difficulty with alcohol or cocaine, the doctors will naturally ask them what other drugs they were using. If they mention marijuana, then this goes down as a "marijuana episode." A few thousand people go to emergency rooms every year for marijuana panic reactions.

This brings up the second point. There is an enormous qualitative difference in the seriousness of the reasons for seeking emergency room treatment. Problems with heroin and cocaine can be fatal. Problems with marijuana are never fatal and are almost always transitory.

Finally, take these numbers at face value and look at them even without knowing what they mean. Never mind the qualitative difference in the problems. And never mind that there are millions of "alcohol related episodes," which somehow they forgot to mention. And never mind the emphysema attacks by chronic tobacco addicts.

There were half again as many "heroin-related episodes" as "marijuana-related eprisodes." But there are 20 to 60 times as many marijuana users as heroin users. Their own numbers tell them that – even without the qualitative differences and even without knowing that these are mentions, not causes – heroin sends 30 to 90 times as many people, per user, to the hospital as marijuana. Now think about the statement that "there is no such thing as a soft-drug." Does the expression "sending the wrong message" ring a bell?
